appraisal_events.evidence: Swann "se sentit déborder de tendresse pour elle" as she leaves the omnibus; the narrator credits her as "meilleur thérapeute que n'eût été son mari", having grafted normal feelings of gratitude and friendship onto his sick love.
appraisal_events.explanation: Mme Cottard is genuinely credited with a curative effect on Swann and placed above her physician husband, but the elevation is delivered comically — her glove releases "une vision de haute vie" mixed with the smell of the dry-cleaner's, and she marches off with her aigrette held high.

appraisal_events.evidence: Odette is being made "plus humaine (plus semblable aux autres femmes)"; jealousy returns only as a faint agreeable tickle, and when Swann stumbles on proof that Forcheville had been her lover "il s'aperçut qu'il n'en ressentait aucune douleur, que l'amour était loin maintenant".
appraisal_events.explanation: The narrator stages the extinction of Odette's power over Swann: she is de-idealized into an ordinary woman who can no longer inflict pain, and the Odette who inspired love is spoken of as already dead.

appraisal_events.evidence: In the dream Odette looks at her watch, says "Il faut que je m'en aille", and takes leave of everyone alike, "sans prendre à part Swann, sans lui dire où elle le reverrait"; he dares not ask, must smile at Mme Verdurin while his heart pounds, and the dream then declares her the mistress of the Forcheville-figure.
appraisal_events.explanation: The dream restages Swann in his old position of humiliated dependence — undifferentiated in her farewell, unable to follow, ashamed in his nightshirt — though the narrator immediately explains the whole scene as Swann's own false deductions in sleep.

status_effects.explanation: She comes off well locally: credited with a real therapeutic effect on Swann and with inspiring his warmest feeling, even as her grandeur is gently mocked.
Odette is locally reduced from an object of love and torment to a woman like any other, no longer able to move Swann even when proof of her infidelity surfaces.
Swann gains leverage in the relation simply by ceasing to need Odette: her infidelity no longer wounds him and his jealousy has become a pleasant residual sensation.
In the separate movement of the dream he is back at the losing end — not singled out in her goodbye, afraid to ask, hating her while obliged to smile at someone else.

ambiguities: Swann's release from love is double-edged: the narrator's images of the sleeping traveller carried away from a country he meant to bid farewell to, and of the lorgnon wiped and put away in the dark, present the end of his suffering as a numbed loss as much as a gain, so the positive emotional movement should not be read as triumph.
